sources.claim: A debugger pauses controlled execution to inspect frames, variables, and control flow against a stated hypothesis, using breakpoints and stepping as observations rather than random exploration.

canonicalExplanation.summary: A **debugger** pauses your program so you can look inside: the **call stack** (which function called which), **local variables**, and the path the code actually takes. Use it **with a hypothesis**, not as a random walk: "I think `count` is 0 when the list is empty". Set a **breakpoint** just before the suspect line (or a **conditional breakpoint** like `items.length === 0`), run the failing case, inspect, then **step over** (next line), **step into** (enter a call) or **continue** (run to the next breakpoint). Write down what you observed. It either confirms the hypothesis or points to the next one.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A stats page shows `NaN` for some users. A learner starts the debugger at the top of the app and presses "step" 300 times, getting lost in framework code. A breakpoint before a failing division confirms the denominator becomes zero only on empty input, supporting one specific guard hypothesis. In this lesson you'll record and explain a debugger-assisted root-cause investigation.


sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Dependencies and reproducible builds**, **Commits and history**, **Debugging and testing loop** (reproducing a failure) and **Build and task commands**.

sections.heading: The model: hypothesis, breakpoint, observation
sections.body:
```js
function average(scores) {
  const total = scores.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
  const count = scores.length;
  return total / count;          // breakpoint here, condition: count === 0.
}
```

```text
Hypothesis: NaN appears when scores is empty.
Run the failing case (a user with no scores) under the debugger.
Paused at line 4.
  Call stack:  average <- renderStats <- onLoad.
  Variables:   scores = [], total = 0, count = 0.
Observation: 0 / 0 = NaN. Hypothesis confirmed.
Next: guard empty input; add a test for [].
```

| Control | Does |
|---|---|
| step over. | run the current line, stop at the next. |
| step into. | enter the function called on this line. |
| step out. | finish this function, stop in its caller. |
| continue. | run until the next breakpoint. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why a conditional breakpoint?", "answer": "average() may run hundreds of times with valid data. The condition pauses only on the interesting case, so you don't click through every call."}
```

sections.heading: Record what you saw

includes: Form a hypothesis, set breakpoints near the symptom, and inspect stack and variables.
Use step over, into, out and continue, and record each observation.

outcomes: Record and explain a debugger-assisted root-cause investigation.

examples.title: The average that divides by zero
examples.situation: A breakpoint before a failing division confirms the denominator becomes zero only on empty input, supporting one specific guard hypothesis.
walkthrough: **A breakpoint before a failing division:** conditional breakpoint on line 4 with count === 0.
**Confirms the denominator becomes zero only on empty input:** paused with scores = [] and count = 0; valid users never hit it.
**Supporting one specific guard hypothesis:** return null for empty input and show "No scores yet"; a test for [] will prove it.
examples.result: The root cause is identified and recorded in minutes, with a targeted fix and test.

examples.title: The wrong discount
examples.situation: An order total is 10% too high. The learner hypothesises the discount isn't applied.
walkthrough: Breakpoint in applyDiscount: it's never hit.
Call stack at the total shows checkout skips it when a coupon has uppercase letters.
New hypothesis: case-sensitive coupon check; confirmed by inspecting the comparison.
examples.result: Two hypotheses, two observations, one clear root cause.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: The best debugging strategy is to step through every line from program start until something looks suspicious.
misconceptions.correction: Stepping without a hypothesis wastes time in unrelated code. Start near the symptom, predict what you'll see, and let each observation confirm or reject the idea.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening story, why did 300 steps not help?

analogy.example: Debugging with a hypothesis is like **a detective checking one alibi at a time**. You don't interview the whole city; you ask "was the suspect at the station at 9?" and check the camera at exactly that moment (breakpoint).
usefulFor: remembering one alibi at a time
limitations: Detectives can't rerun the crime; you can rerun the program.
A broken alibi still moves the case forward.

remediation.explanation: Before touching the debugger write: **I think ___ because ___; I'll pause at ___ and expect to see ___.** Then compare.

recap.summary: To record a debugger-assisted root-cause investigation, state a hypothesis, set a breakpoint (conditional if needed) just before the suspect line, run the failing case, inspect the call stack and variables, step deliberately, and write down each observation until the cause is confirmed and a fix and test follow.
